paper.title: Discontinuity in care: Practice closures among primary care providers and patient health care utilization
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement and no Statistics Denmark project reference are printed. …

registers.role: treatment (patient‒practice links and closure dates), sample frame, outcomes (PCP visits and government reimbursement)
outcomes (hospital interactions: outpatient care and inpatient admissions with cardiovascular, diabetes-related and cancer diagnoses)
linkage (identifies the physicians associated with each practice)

registers.name_in_paper: A Statistics Denmark dataset of address-speciﬁc geocode-based distances between individuals and the (up to) 50 closest physicians within a 20 km travel distance
registers.role: outcome (distance to physician) and construction of patient choice sets / patient density
variables_mentioned: distance in km using public roads

linkages: Patients linked to their primary care practice through patient‒physician interactions in the fee-for-service data, using an algorithm in line with Kjærsgaard et al. (2016), which links individuals to their practice in 98.6% of all cases
Physicians linked to practices through Yderregisteret
Individuals linked to physician distances through address-speciﬁc geocodes (2004‒2010)
Patients linked to hospital interactions and ICD10 diagnoses through Landspatientregisteret
Practices linked to one another through observed patient mobility, to identify practice ﬁxed eﬀects within a connected set (99.3% of the sample)

sample.universe: The entire adult (18+) population of Denmark covered by Danish administrative registers, 1998‒2015
sample.unit_of_observation: Individual by quarter (quarterly bins in a four-year window around the (synthetic) practice closure)
selection_rules: Start from patient‒physician spells covering 1998‒2015, with practice identity inferred from patient‒physician interactions
Deﬁne a practice as closing in the last month in which patient‒practice contact is observed
Keep individuals exposed to a practice closure: roughly 20% of the adult population, 811,649 individuals across 770 closing practices
Use only the ﬁrst practice closure (6.5% of individuals experience multiple closures)
Treat patients listed at a closing clinic up to six months before the closure as treated individuals

Match to a comparison group of 877,547 individuals (across 915 practices) who experience a practice closure three years into the future, assigned a synthetic (random) closing date in the year of the match drawn from the empirical distribution of observed closing dates
Construct a balanced quarterly panel over a four-year window around the (synthetic) closure (two years before and after)
Drop the quarter immediately prior to closure (t = -1); treat everything prior to it as pre-closure

In the models of Tables A1 and A2, drop individuals with missing values in any of the variables in Table 1 (about 35,000 quarter-by-individual observations, a fraction of 0.001 of the original sample)
For the distance analysis, restrict to the 261,166 of 530,594 individuals experiencing a closure from 2005 to 2010 for whom changes in distance can be identiﬁed
For the retirement analysis, split closures by an imputed closing-physician age threshold of 60.3 years
For practice-style estimation, restrict to the largest set of providers connected through pre-closure patient mobility (99.3% of the sample)
sample.n_observations: 25,302,769 quarter by individual observations in the main estimation sample (24,844,530 in Table 3 columns 4‒6; 18,262,557 in the distance sample of Table 3 columns 1‒3; 20,156,712 for retirement closures and 17,761,015 for non-retirement closures)
sample.n_individuals: 811,649 individuals exposed to a practice closure (across 770 closing practices) and 877,547 comparison individuals (across 915 practices); 2,826 destination practices

construction_notes: A practice is deﬁned as closing in the last month in which patient‒practice contact is observed; online supplement Figure B1 shows corresponding reductions in practice-level reimbursement leading up to the closure
Patients at a closing clinic up to six months before the closure are treated, because practice size is roughly constant until about six months before closing (Fig. 1)

The comparison group is assigned a synthetic (random) closing date in the year of the match, drawn from the empirical distribution of observed closing dates, to avoid conflating seasonal variation with behavioral responses
Analysis is on quarterly bins over a four-year window around the closure; quarter t = -1 is dropped from the formal analyses
In the event studies, t = -2 is the reference quarter and eﬀects are measured relative to the quarterly mean in the penultimate year prior to closing (quarters -8 to -4 inclusive)
Initiations of drug therapy are deﬁned as ﬁrst prescriptions since 1995, so restarts after a long period of non-adherence are not counted
The destination practice is the ﬁrst practice with whom a patient interacts after leaving a closing practice

Patient density is the ratio of practices in the patient's choice set that is closed for the intake of new patients; a practice is approximated as closed for intake if the patients-to-physician ratio is larger than 1600
Retirement-driven closures are identiﬁed by imputing (Hastie et al., 2001) an age threshold of 60.3 years from the ages of the closing physicians

Practice styles are provider ﬁxed eﬀects from the two-way ﬁxed-eﬀects model y_ijt = α_i + γ_j + τ_t + ε_ijt estimated on pre-closure data, with periods around the break-up of the patient‒physician relationship dummied out

Practice-style estimates are corrected for measurement error by a split-sample procedure (Drenik et al., 2020): the sample is split at random into two groups, ﬁxed eﬀects γ̂_j^1 and γ̂_j^2 are estimated on each, and the predicted values from a regression of γ̂_j^1 on γ̂_j^2 are used as shrunken estimates

Tables A1‒A4 print coeﬃcients and mean outcomes labelled '(x100)'; for the 0/1 indicator outcomes this makes the printed coeﬃcients percentage points, while for the DKK columns the scaling is inconsistent with the magnitudes quoted in the text
Standard errors are clustered on the practice level in Table 3 and Tables A1‒A2 and on the physician level in Tables A3‒A4

claims.statement: Exposure to a primary care practice closure increases Distance to physician (km) in the two years following the closure, among individuals aged 18+ listed with a danish primary care practice that closes between 2005 and 2010 and for whom distance changes are identiﬁed.

treatment.label: Closure X Post (exposure to a primary care practice closure, post-closure period)

register_source.value: Sygesikringsregisteret (fee-for-service data; patient‒physician interactions used to infer practice identity); Yderregisteret (physicians associated with each practice)

definition.value: Indicator for belonging to the group exposed to the practice closure, interacted with an indicator for the post-closure period. A practice is deﬁned as closing in the last month in which patient‒practice contact is observed; patients listed at a closing clinic up to six months before the closure are treated. The comparison group consists of individuals who experience a practice closure three years into the future and is assigned a synthetic (random) closing date in the year of the match, drawn from the empirical distribution of observed closing dates. Only the ﬁrst practice closure is used.

timing.value: Closure at event time t = 0; quarterly bins in a four-year window around the (synthetic) closure, quarter t = -1 dropped, everything prior to it treated as pre-closure; 'Post' covers quarters 0 to +7

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark address-speciﬁc geocode-based distance dataset (2004‒2010)

definition.value: Road-distance in km between the individual's home address and the primary care physician, from the Statistics Denmark geocode-based dataset covering distances between the home addresses of all individuals and the (up to) 50 closest physicians within a 20 km travel distance using public roads (available 2004‒2010)

timing.value: Measured per quarter over a four-year window around the (synthetic) closure; the post-closure period covers quarters 0 to +7

units.value: km

magnitude.interpretation: Although statistically signiﬁcant, we ﬁnd no economically important increases in distance arising from practice closure. On average, patients travel 0.5 km longer.

estimand.target_population: Individuals aged 18+ listed with a Danish primary care practice that closes between 2005 and 2010 and for whom distance changes are identiﬁed
estimand.time_horizon: Average eﬀect over the post-closure period (quarters 0 to +7, i.e. the two years following the (synthetic) closure)

population.description: The distance sample: the 261,166 of 530,594 individuals experiencing a practice closure from 2005 to 2010 for whom changes in distance can be identiﬁed from the geocode-based distance data, plus the matched comparison group
subgroups_defined: Retirement-driven vs. non-retirement closures (imputed closing-physician age threshold of 60.3 years)
Quintiles of the share of practices in the patient's choice set closed for intake (patient density)
population.selection: Conditioned on being listed with a primary care practice that closes within the observation window: the exposed group experiences the closure now, the comparison group three years later. Only the ﬁrst closure is used; in Tables A1 and A2 individuals with missing values in any Table 1 variable are dropped (about 35,000 quarter-by-individual observations, a fraction of 0.001).

identification.source_of_variation: The timing of closures of Danish primary care practices over 1998‒2015 (770 closing practices), with patients at practices that close three years later as the comparison group and a synthetic closing date drawn from the empirical distribution of observed closing dates

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: in the absence of practice closure there are no diﬀerential trends in outcomes between the treatment group and the comparison group (individuals whose practice closes three years later).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Event-study ﬁgures showing constant pre-closure eﬀects (Fig. 2, Fig. 3); robustness to varying the choice of reference period; placebo analyses using outcomes measured prior to the actual closing

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation in the pre-period used for comparison: patients do not react to the upcoming closure before the dropped quarter, so pre-closure quarters are uncontaminated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 on net patient ﬂows leading up to closure (practice size roughly constant until six months before closing); quarter t = -1 is dropped and patients are counted as treated from six months before the closure

key_assumptions.assumption: Individuals whose practice closes three years into the future are a valid comparison group; the estimation sample is conditioned on eventually experiencing a practice closure.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 shows the exposed group resembles the comparison group on observed pre-closure characteristics; the synthetic closing dates are drawn from the empirical distribution of observed closing dates to avoid conflating seasonality

implies_edges.from: eventual practice closure (within the observation window)

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: outcomes of comparison individuals are not aﬀected by the closures experienced by the treated individuals (e.g. through crowding of destination practices).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 2 shows destination practices do not experience large inﬂows of patients following closures of nearby practices; Table 3 shows no statistically signiﬁcant eﬀect on patients per physician

key_assumptions.assumption: Access to primary care is maintained for every patient when a practice closes, so the estimates capture the discontinuity itself rather than loss of access; to the extent that care in government-established clinics is of lower quality this is part of the estimated eﬀect.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Institutional description (the local governments are obligated by law to guarantee access); no statistically signiﬁcant reduction in PCP visits; Fig. A4 shows eﬀects on PCP utilization do not decrease with the share of nearby practices closed for intake

threats_discussed: Patients enrolled in practices that close may comprise a diﬀerent population than patients enrolled in practices that continue to operate
Patient anticipation of the closure (patients leaving the practice before it closes, and those leavers diﬀering on observables)
Destination PCPs could be capacity-constrained and unable to deliver services on par with the closing physicians
Increases in distance to the new practice and in the patient load of the new provider
Nearby practices being closed for patient intake (access problems in areas with few practices)
Lower service quality in government-established clinics, which would be part of the estimated eﬀects
robustness_checks: Gradually richer speciﬁcations: quarter-relative-to-event and region dummies, then individual background characteristics, then individual ﬁxed eﬀects (columns 1‒3 of each outcome block)
Moving the pre-closure reference period back by three quarters and excluding the interval between it and the actual closure
Placebo analyses using outcomes measured prior to the actual closing (online supplement Tables B1‒B2)
Replication of the diﬀerence-in-diﬀerences strategy on the distance sample (online supplement Table B4)
Correcting for missing values by including dummies for missing values
Separating retirement-driven from non-retirement closures (Tables A3 and A4)
unresolved_confounders: The quality of service received in government-established clinics, which 'will comprise part of the eﬀects we estimate in our analyses below'
The relative weights of provider practice style versus disruption, which the authors state they cannot answer in a causal sense

estimator.value: OLS diﬀerence-in-diﬀerences with individual ﬁxed eﬀects

estimation.specification: Minimalist diﬀerence-in-diﬀerences: 'Closure X Post' with quarter-relative-to-event dummies, region dummies, individual background characteristics and individual ﬁxed eﬀects (Table 3, col (3)); the paper's main model is the event-study equation (1), and the minimalist model 'do[es] not allow eﬀects of closure to vary with distance to the event'
controls: Individual background characteristics (reported in the table as 'Individual background chars: Yes'; not itemized in the paper)

source_table.value: Table 3, col (3), row 'Closure X Post'

adjustment_set.label: Individual background characteristics (not itemized in the paper)

nodes: eventual practice closure (within the observation window)

edges.from: eventual practice closure (within the observation window)

ambiguities: The point estimate is read from the 'Closure X Post' row of the richest speciﬁcation for this outcome (the column with individual ﬁxed eﬀects); the paper presents columns 1‒3 of each outcome block as a 'gradually richer speciﬁcation' and does not single one out as preferred.

The estimating equation printed in the paper is the event-study equation (1); no equation is printed for the minimalist diﬀerence-in-diﬀerence model whose 'Closure X Post' coeﬃcient the tables report, and the ﬁgure notes refer to that model as 'speciﬁcation (2)' while equation (2) in the text is the two-way ﬁxed-eﬀects practice-style model.

Table 3 also reports a 'Closure' level coeﬃcient of 3.46 (SE 0.08) against a mean outcome of 3.4 km, implying a large pre-closure level diﬀerence in distance between exposed and comparison individuals; the paper does not discuss this coeﬃcient.
The printed 'Mean outcome' of 3.4 km is not labelled as a treatment- or comparison-group mean; it is recorded here as the baseline mean of the outcome.

population.description: Individuals exposed to a primary care practice closure in Denmark 1998‒2015 (811,649 individuals distributed across 770 closing practices) and a matched comparison group of 877,547 individuals who experience a practice closure three years into the future (915 practices); quarterly observations in a four-year window around the (synthetic) closure

implies_edges.from: eventual practice closure (within the observation window)

definition.value: Indicator for belonging to the group exposed to the practice closure, interacted with an indicator for the post-closure period. definition.value: Indicator for belonging to the group exposed to the practice closure, interacted with an indicator for the post-closure period. timing.value: Measured per quarter over a four-year window around the (synthetic) closure; the post-closure period covers quarters 0 to +7

units.value: percentage points: the table rows are labelled 'Closure X Post (x100)' and 'Mean outcome (x100)', and the outcome is a 0/1 quarterly indicator, so the printed coeﬃcient is the eﬀect multiplied by 100

estimand.target_population: Individuals aged 18+ listed with a Danish primary care practice that closes, and individuals listed with a practice that closes three years later

population.description: Individuals exposed to a primary care practice closure in Denmark 1998‒2015 (811,649 individuals distributed across 770 closing practices) and a matched comparison group of 877,547 individuals who experience a practice closure three years into the future (915 practices); quarterly observations in a four-year window around the (synthetic) closure
subgroups_defined: Retirement-driven vs. non-retirement closures (imputed closing-physician age threshold of 60.3 years)
Quintiles of the share of practices in the patient's choice set closed for intake (patient density)

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: outcomes of comparison individuals are not aﬀected by the closures experienced by the treated individuals (e.g. through crowding of destination practices).

Physician practice style (Chandra et al., 2011)

claims.statement: Exposure to a primary care practice closure has no detectable effect on Diab Hosp >5 days (diabetes-related inpatient admission lasting more than 5 days) in the two years following the closure, among individuals aged 18+ listed with a danish primary care practice that closes, and individuals listed with a practice that closes three years later.

treatment.label: Closure X Post (exposure to a primary care practice closure, post-closure period)

register_source.value: Sygesikringsregisteret (fee-for-service data; patient‒physician interactions used to infer practice identity); Yderregisteret (physicians associated with each practice)

definition.value: Indicator for belonging to the group exposed to the practice closure, interacted with an indicator for the post-closure period. A practice is deﬁned as closing in the last month in which patient‒practice contact is observed; patients listed at a closing clinic up to six months before the closure are treated. The comparison group consists of individuals who experience a practice closure three years into the future and is assigned a synthetic (random) closing date in the year of the match, drawn from the empirical distribution of observed closing dates. Only the ﬁrst practice closure is used.

timing.value: Closure at event time t = 0; quarterly bins in a four-year window around the (synthetic) closure, quarter t = -1 dropped, everything prior to it treated as pre-closure; 'Post' covers quarters 0 to +7

outcome.label: Diab Hosp >5 days (diabetes-related inpatient admission lasting more than 5 days)

register_source.value: Landspatientregisteret (health care service use and ICD10-diagnoses associated with hospital interactions)

definition.value: Indicator (0/1) for a diabetes-related inpatient admission lasting more than 5 days in the quarter; admissions are also considered by length of admission

timing.value: Measured per quarter over a four-year window around the (synthetic) closure; the post-closure period covers quarters 0 to +7

units.value: percentage points: the table rows are labelled 'Closure X Post (x100)' and 'Mean outcome (x100)', and the outcome is a 0/1 quarterly indicator, so the printed coeﬃcient is the eﬀect multiplied by 100

estimand.target_population: Individuals aged 18+ listed with a Danish primary care practice that closes, and individuals listed with a practice that closes three years later
estimand.time_horizon: Average eﬀect over the post-closure period (quarters 0 to +7, i.e. the two years following the (synthetic) closure)

population.description: Individuals exposed to a primary care practice closure in Denmark 1998‒2015 (811,649 individuals distributed across 770 closing practices) and a matched comparison group of 877,547 individuals who experience a practice closure three years into the future (915 practices); quarterly observations in a four-year window around the (synthetic) closure
subgroups_defined: Retirement-driven vs. non-retirement closures (imputed closing-physician age threshold of 60.3 years)
Quintiles of the share of practices in the patient's choice set closed for intake (patient density)
population.selection: Conditioned on being listed with a primary care practice that closes within the observation window: the exposed group experiences the closure now, the comparison group three years later. Only the ﬁrst closure is used; in Tables A1 and A2 individuals with missing values in any Table 1 variable are dropped (about 35,000 quarter-by-individual observations, a fraction of 0.001).

identification.source_of_variation: The timing of closures of Danish primary care practices over 1998‒2015 (770 closing practices), with patients at practices that close three years later as the comparison group and a synthetic closing date drawn from the empirical distribution of observed closing dates

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: in the absence of practice closure there are no diﬀerential trends in outcomes between the treatment group and the comparison group (individuals whose practice closes three years later).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Event-study ﬁgures showing constant pre-closure eﬀects (Fig. 2, Fig. 3); robustness to varying the choice of reference period; placebo analyses using outcomes measured prior to the actual closing

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation in the pre-period used for comparison: patients do not react to the upcoming closure before the dropped quarter, so pre-closure quarters are uncontaminated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 on net patient ﬂows leading up to closure (practice size roughly constant until six months before closing); quarter t = -1 is dropped and patients are counted as treated from six months before the closure

key_assumptions.assumption: Individuals whose practice closes three years into the future are a valid comparison group; the estimation sample is conditioned on eventually experiencing a practice closure.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 shows the exposed group resembles the comparison group on observed pre-closure characteristics; the synthetic closing dates are drawn from the empirical distribution of observed closing dates to avoid conflating seasonality

implies_edges.from: eventual practice closure (within the observation window)

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: outcomes of comparison individuals are not aﬀected by the closures experienced by the treated individuals (e.g. through crowding of destination practices).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 2 shows destination practices do not experience large inﬂows of patients following closures of nearby practices; Table 3 shows no statistically signiﬁcant eﬀect on patients per physician

key_assumptions.assumption: Access to primary care is maintained for every patient when a practice closes, so the estimates capture the discontinuity itself rather than loss of access; to the extent that care in government-established clinics is of lower quality this is part of the estimated eﬀect.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Institutional description (the local governments are obligated by law to guarantee access); no statistically signiﬁcant reduction in PCP visits; Fig. A4 shows eﬀects on PCP utilization do not decrease with the share of nearby practices closed for intake

threats_discussed: Patients enrolled in practices that close may comprise a diﬀerent population than patients enrolled in practices that continue to operate
Patient anticipation of the closure (patients leaving the practice before it closes, and those leavers diﬀering on observables)
Destination PCPs could be capacity-constrained and unable to deliver services on par with the closing physicians
Increases in distance to the new practice and in the patient load of the new provider
Nearby practices being closed for patient intake (access problems in areas with few practices)
Lower service quality in government-established clinics, which would be part of the estimated eﬀects
robustness_checks: Gradually richer speciﬁcations: quarter-relative-to-event and region dummies, then individual background characteristics, then individual ﬁxed eﬀects (columns 1‒3 of each outcome block)
Moving the pre-closure reference period back by three quarters and excluding the interval between it and the actual closure
Placebo analyses using outcomes measured prior to the actual closing (online supplement Tables B1‒B2)
Replication of the diﬀerence-in-diﬀerences strategy on the distance sample (online supplement Table B4)
Correcting for missing values by including dummies for missing values
Separating retirement-driven from non-retirement closures (Tables A3 and A4)
unresolved_confounders: The quality of service received in government-established clinics, which 'will comprise part of the eﬀects we estimate in our analyses below'
The relative weights of provider practice style versus disruption, which the authors state they cannot answer in a causal sense

estimator.value: OLS diﬀerence-in-diﬀerences with individual ﬁxed eﬀects (linear probability model for the 0/1 outcomes)

estimation.specification: Minimalist diﬀerence-in-diﬀerences: 'Closure X Post' with quarter-relative-to-event dummies, region dummies, individual background characteristics and individual ﬁxed eﬀects (Table A2, Panel B, col (6)); the paper's main model is the event-study equation (1), and the minimalist model 'do[es] not allow eﬀects of closure to vary with distance to the event'
controls: Individual background characteristics (reported in the table as 'Individual background chars: Yes'; not itemized in the paper)

source_table.value: Table A2, Panel B, col (6), row 'Closure X Post'

adjustment_set.label: Individual background characteristics (not itemized in the paper)

heterogeneity.dimension: Length of admission (any admission vs. >5 days vs. >10 days)
heterogeneity.finding: For cardiovascular and diabetes-related admissions the eﬀects are concentrated on any admission, with no statistically signiﬁcant eﬀects for admissions lasting more than 5 or more than 10 days; for cancer the eﬀects are statistically signiﬁcant at all three admission lengths (Table A2)

nodes: Diab Hosp >5 days (diabetes-related inpatient admission lasting more than 5 days)
eventual practice closure (within the observation window)

edges.to: Diab Hosp >5 days (diabetes-related inpatient admission lasting more than 5 days)

edges.from: eventual practice closure (within the observation window)

edges.to: Diab Hosp >5 days (diabetes-related inpatient admission lasting more than 5 days)
Diab Hosp >5 days (diabetes-related inpatient admission lasting more than 5 days)
Diab Hosp >5 days (diabetes-related inpatient admission lasting more than 5 days)

ambiguities: The point estimate is read from the 'Closure X Post' row of the richest speciﬁcation for this outcome (the column with individual ﬁxed eﬀects); the paper presents columns 1‒3 of each outcome block as a 'gradually richer speciﬁcation' and does not single one out as preferred.

The estimating equation printed in the paper is the event-study equation (1); no equation is printed for the minimalist diﬀerence-in-diﬀerence model whose 'Closure X Post' coeﬃcient the tables report, and the ﬁgure notes refer to that model as 'speciﬁcation (2)' while equation (2) in the text is the two-way ﬁxed-eﬀects practice-style model.
The 'Closure' level coeﬃcient in column (4) is printed in scientiﬁc notation as 5.41e-05** (SE 0.002).

claims.statement: Exposure to a primary care practice closure has no detectable effect on Any PCP visit in the two years following the closure, among individuals aged 18+ whose primary care practice closes because the physician retires.

treatment.label: Closure X Post, retirement-driven closure (closing physician older than the imputed 60.3-year age threshold)

register_source.value: Sygesikringsregisteret (fee-for-service data; patient‒physician interactions used to infer practice identity); Yderregisteret (physicians associated with each practice)

definition.value: Indicator for belonging to the group exposed to the practice closure, interacted with an indicator for the post-closure period. A practice is deﬁned as closing in the last month in which patient‒practice contact is observed; patients listed at a closing clinic up to six months before the closure are treated. The comparison group consists of individuals who experience a practice closure three years into the future and is assigned a synthetic (random) closing date in the year of the match, drawn from the empirical distribution of observed closing dates. Only the ﬁrst practice closure is used. In Table A3 the sample is restricted to individuals experiencing a closure classiﬁed as due to physician retirement: an age threshold of 60.3 years is imputed from the ages of the closing physicians and physicians older than the threshold are classiﬁed as retirees.

timing.value: Closure at event time t = 0; quarterly bins in a four-year window around the (synthetic) closure, quarter t = -1 dropped, everything prior to it treated as pre-closure; 'Post' covers quarters 0 to +7

register_source.value: Sygesikringsregisteret (fee-for-service data on reimbursements paid to all PCPs)

definition.value: Indicator (0/1) for any consultation with the primary care physician in the quarter; primary care utilization is measured via indicators for physician visits

timing.value: Measured per quarter over a four-year window around the (synthetic) closure; the post-closure period covers quarters 0 to +7

units.value: percentage points: the table rows are labelled 'Closure X Post (x100)' and 'Mean outcome (x100)', and the outcome is a 0/1 quarterly indicator, so the printed coeﬃcient is the eﬀect multiplied by 100

magnitude.interpretation: We ﬁnd that while the diﬀerences in eﬀects are miniscule for the primary care utilization and secondary care, the eﬀects on initiation with chronic medication are signiﬁcantly lower (by a factor 3) for the sample of individuals who experience a closure due to non-retirement.

estimand.target_population: Individuals aged 18+ whose primary care practice closes because the physician retires
estimand.time_horizon: Average eﬀect over the post-closure period (quarters 0 to +7, i.e. the two years following the (synthetic) closure)

population.description: Individuals experiencing a practice closure classiﬁed as retirement-driven (closing physician older than the imputed age threshold of 60.3 years), plus matched comparison individuals; quarterly observations in a four-year window around the (synthetic) closure
subgroups_defined: Retirement-driven vs. non-retirement closures (imputed closing-physician age threshold of 60.3 years)
Quintiles of the share of practices in the patient's choice set closed for intake (patient density)
population.selection: Conditioned on being listed with a primary care practice that closes within the observation window: the exposed group experiences the closure now, the comparison group three years later. Only the ﬁrst closure is used; in Tables A1 and A2 individuals with missing values in any Table 1 variable are dropped (about 35,000 quarter-by-individual observations, a fraction of 0.001).

identification.source_of_variation: The timing of closures of Danish primary care practices over 1998‒2015 (770 closing practices), with patients at practices that close three years later as the comparison group and a synthetic closing date drawn from the empirical distribution of observed closing dates

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: in the absence of practice closure there are no diﬀerential trends in outcomes between the treatment group and the comparison group (individuals whose practice closes three years later).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Event-study ﬁgures showing constant pre-closure eﬀects (Fig. 2, Fig. 3); robustness to varying the choice of reference period; placebo analyses using outcomes measured prior to the actual closing

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation in the pre-period used for comparison: patients do not react to the upcoming closure before the dropped quarter, so pre-closure quarters are uncontaminated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 on net patient ﬂows leading up to closure (practice size roughly constant until six months before closing); quarter t = -1 is dropped and patients are counted as treated from six months before the closure

key_assumptions.assumption: Individuals whose practice closes three years into the future are a valid comparison group; the estimation sample is conditioned on eventually experiencing a practice closure.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 shows the exposed group resembles the comparison group on observed pre-closure characteristics; the synthetic closing dates are drawn from the empirical distribution of observed closing dates to avoid conflating seasonality

implies_edges.from: eventual practice closure (within the observation window)

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: outcomes of comparison individuals are not aﬀected by the closures experienced by the treated individuals (e.g. through crowding of destination practices).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 2 shows destination practices do not experience large inﬂows of patients following closures of nearby practices; Table 3 shows no statistically signiﬁcant eﬀect on patients per physician

key_assumptions.assumption: Access to primary care is maintained for every patient when a practice closes, so the estimates capture the discontinuity itself rather than loss of access; to the extent that care in government-established clinics is of lower quality this is part of the estimated eﬀect.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Institutional description (the local governments are obligated by law to guarantee access); no statistically signiﬁcant reduction in PCP visits; Fig. A4 shows eﬀects on PCP utilization do not decrease with the share of nearby practices closed for intake

key_assumptions.assumption: The imputed closing-physician age threshold of 60.3 years correctly separates retirement-driven closures from closures for other reasons (the reason for closure is not observed in the data).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imputation following Hastie et al. (2001), described in online supplement D and illustrated in online supplement Figure B4; online supplement Figures B5 and B6 show the two closure types do not diﬀer in patient anticipation

threats_discussed: Patients enrolled in practices that close may comprise a diﬀerent population than patients enrolled in practices that continue to operate
Patient anticipation of the closure (patients leaving the practice before it closes, and those leavers diﬀering on observables)

Increases in distance to the new practice and in the patient load of the new provider
Nearby practices being closed for patient intake (access problems in areas with few practices)
Lower service quality in government-established clinics, which would be part of the estimated eﬀects

Placebo analyses using outcomes measured prior to the actual closing (online supplement Tables B1‒B2)

Correcting for missing values by including dummies for missing values
Separating retirement-driven from non-retirement closures (Tables A3 and A4)
unresolved_confounders: The quality of service received in government-established clinics, which 'will comprise part of the eﬀects we estimate in our analyses below'
The relative weights of provider practice style versus disruption, which the authors state they cannot answer in a causal sense

estimator.value: OLS diﬀerence-in-diﬀerences with individual ﬁxed eﬀects (linear probability model for the 0/1 outcomes)

estimation.specification: Minimalist diﬀerence-in-diﬀerences: 'Closure X Post' with quarter-relative-to-event dummies, region dummies, individual background characteristics and individual ﬁxed eﬀects (Table A3, Panel A, col (3)); the paper's main model is the event-study equation (1), and the minimalist model 'do[es] not allow eﬀects of closure to vary with distance to the event'
controls: Individual background characteristics (reported in the table as 'Individual background chars: Yes'; not itemized in the paper)

source_table.value: Table A3, Panel A, col (3), row 'Closure X Post'

adjustment_set.label: Individual background characteristics (not itemized in the paper)

heterogeneity.dimension: Reason for closure (physician retirement vs. other reasons)
heterogeneity.finding: This estimate is for retirement-driven closures; the corresponding non-retirement estimate is in Table A4. The paper states that individuals experiencing closures classiﬁed as retirements face a much larger reduction in physician age (16 years vs. 3.5 years) and a larger increase in the occurrence of female physicians (14 vs. 0.4 percentage points)

nodes: eventual practice closure (within the observation window)

edges.from: eventual practice closure (within the observation window)

ambiguities: The point estimate is read from the 'Closure X Post' row of the richest speciﬁcation for this outcome (the column with individual ﬁxed eﬀects); the paper presents columns 1‒3 of each outcome block as a 'gradually richer speciﬁcation' and does not single one out as preferred.

The estimating equation printed in the paper is the event-study equation (1); no equation is printed for the minimalist diﬀerence-in-diﬀerence model whose 'Closure X Post' coeﬃcient the tables report, and the ﬁgure notes refer to that model as 'speciﬁcation (2)' while equation (2) in the text is the two-way ﬁxed-eﬀects practice-style model.

definition.value: Indicator for belonging to the group exposed to the practice closure, interacted with an indicator for the post-closure period. claims.statement: Exposure to a primary care practice closure increases Metformin (initiation with metformin) in the two years following the closure, among individuals aged 18+ whose primary care practice closes because the physician retires.

treatment.label: Closure X Post, retirement-driven closure (closing physician older than the imputed 60.3-year age threshold)

register_source.value: Sygesikringsregisteret (fee-for-service data; patient‒physician interactions used to infer practice identity); Yderregisteret (physicians associated with each practice)

definition.value: Indicator for belonging to the group exposed to the practice closure, interacted with an indicator for the post-closure period. A practice is deﬁned as closing in the last month in which patient‒practice contact is observed; patients listed at a closing clinic up to six months before the closure are treated. The comparison group consists of individuals who experience a practice closure three years into the future and is assigned a synthetic (random) closing date in the year of the match, drawn from the empirical distribution of observed closing dates. Only the ﬁrst practice closure is used. In Table A3 the sample is restricted to individuals experiencing a closure classiﬁed as due to physician retirement: an age threshold of 60.3 years is imputed from the ages of the closing physicians and physicians older than the threshold are classiﬁed as retirees.

timing.value: Closure at event time t = 0; quarterly bins in a four-year window around the (synthetic) closure, quarter t = -1 dropped, everything prior to it treated as pre-closure; 'Post' covers quarters 0 to +7

definition.value: Indicator (0/1) for initiation of treatment with metformin (ﬁrst-line treatment for type 2 diabetes) in the quarter; initiations are deﬁned as ﬁrst prescriptions since 1995

timing.value: Measured per quarter over a four-year window around the (synthetic) closure; the post-closure period covers quarters 0 to +7

units.value: percentage points: the table rows are labelled 'Closure X Post (x100)' and 'Mean outcome (x100)', and the outcome is a 0/1 quarterly indicator, so the printed coeﬃcient is the eﬀect multiplied by 100

magnitude.interpretation: We ﬁnd that while the diﬀerences in eﬀects are miniscule for the primary care utilization and secondary care, the eﬀects on initiation with chronic medication are signiﬁcantly lower (by a factor 3) for the sample of individuals who experience a closure due to non-retirement.

estimand.target_population: Individuals aged 18+ whose primary care practice closes because the physician retires
estimand.time_horizon: Average eﬀect over the post-closure period (quarters 0 to +7, i.e. the two years following the (synthetic) closure)

population.description: Individuals experiencing a practice closure classiﬁed as retirement-driven (closing physician older than the imputed age threshold of 60.3 years), plus matched comparison individuals; quarterly observations in a four-year window around the (synthetic) closure
subgroups_defined: Retirement-driven vs. non-retirement closures (imputed closing-physician age threshold of 60.3 years)
Quintiles of the share of practices in the patient's choice set closed for intake (patient density)
population.selection: Conditioned on being listed with a primary care practice that closes within the observation window: the exposed group experiences the closure now, the comparison group three years later. Only the ﬁrst closure is used; in Tables A1 and A2 individuals with missing values in any Table 1 variable are dropped (about 35,000 quarter-by-individual observations, a fraction of 0.001).

identification.source_of_variation: The timing of closures of Danish primary care practices over 1998‒2015 (770 closing practices), with patients at practices that close three years later as the comparison group and a synthetic closing date drawn from the empirical distribution of observed closing dates

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: in the absence of practice closure there are no diﬀerential trends in outcomes between the treatment group and the comparison group (individuals whose practice closes three years later).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Event-study ﬁgures showing constant pre-closure eﬀects (Fig. 2, Fig. 3); robustness to varying the choice of reference period; placebo analyses using outcomes measured prior to the actual closing

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation in the pre-period used for comparison: patients do not react to the upcoming closure before the dropped quarter, so pre-closure quarters are uncontaminated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 on net patient ﬂows leading up to closure (practice size roughly constant until six months before closing); quarter t = -1 is dropped and patients are counted as treated from six months before the closure

key_assumptions.assumption: Individuals whose practice closes three years into the future are a valid comparison group; the estimation sample is conditioned on eventually experiencing a practice closure.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 shows the exposed group resembles the comparison group on observed pre-closure characteristics; the synthetic closing dates are drawn from the empirical distribution of observed closing dates to avoid conflating seasonality

implies_edges.from: eventual practice closure (within the observation window)

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: outcomes of comparison individuals are not aﬀected by the closures experienced by the treated individuals (e.g. through crowding of destination practices).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 2 shows destination practices do not experience large inﬂows of patients following closures of nearby practices; Table 3 shows no statistically signiﬁcant eﬀect on patients per physician

key_assumptions.assumption: Access to primary care is maintained for every patient when a practice closes, so the estimates capture the discontinuity itself rather than loss of access; to the extent that care in government-established clinics is of lower quality this is part of the estimated eﬀect.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Institutional description (the local governments are obligated by law to guarantee access); no statistically signiﬁcant reduction in PCP visits; Fig. A4 shows eﬀects on PCP utilization do not decrease with the share of nearby practices closed for intake

key_assumptions.assumption: The imputed closing-physician age threshold of 60.3 years correctly separates retirement-driven closures from closures for other reasons (the reason for closure is not observed in the data).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imputation following Hastie et al. (2001), described in online supplement D and illustrated in online supplement Figure B4; online supplement Figures B5 and B6 show the two closure types do not diﬀer in patient anticipation

nodes: eventual practice closure (within the observation window)

edges.from: eventual practice closure (within the observation window)

ambiguities: The point estimate is read from the 'Closure X Post' row of the richest speciﬁcation for this outcome (the column with individual ﬁxed eﬀects); the paper presents columns 1‒3 of each outcome block as a 'gradually richer speciﬁcation' and does not single one out as preferred.

definition.value: Indicator for belonging to the group exposed to the practice closure, interacted with an indicator for the post-closure period. key_assumptions.assumption: Individuals whose practice closes three years into the future are a valid comparison group; the estimation sample is conditioned on eventually experiencing a practice closure.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 shows the exposed group resembles the comparison group on observed pre-closure characteristics; the synthetic closing dates are drawn from the empirical distribution of observed closing dates to avoid conflating seasonality

implies_edges.from: eventual practice closure (within the observation window)

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: outcomes of comparison individuals are not aﬀected by the closures experienced by the treated individuals (e.g. through crowding of destination practices).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 2 shows destination practices do not experience large inﬂows of patients following closures of nearby practices; Table 3 shows no statistically signiﬁcant eﬀect on patients per physician

key_assumptions.assumption: Access to primary care is maintained for every patient when a practice closes, so the estimates capture the discontinuity itself rather than loss of access; to the extent that care in government-established clinics is of lower quality this is part of the estimated eﬀect.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Institutional description (the local governments are obligated by law to guarantee access); no statistically signiﬁcant reduction in PCP visits; Fig. A4 shows eﬀects on PCP utilization do not decrease with the share of nearby practices closed for intake

key_assumptions.assumption: The imputed closing-physician age threshold of 60.3 years correctly separates retirement-driven closures from closures for other reasons (the reason for closure is not observed in the data).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imputation following Hastie et al. (2001), described in online supplement D and illustrated in online supplement Figure B4; online supplement Figures B5 and B6 show the two closure types do not diﬀer in patient anticipation

threats_discussed: Patients enrolled in practices that close may comprise a diﬀerent population than patients enrolled in practices that continue to operate
Patient anticipation of the closure (patients leaving the practice before it closes, and those leavers diﬀering on observables)
Destination PCPs could be capacity-constrained and unable to deliver services on par with the closing physicians
Increases in distance to the new practice and in the patient load of the new provider
Nearby practices being closed for patient intake (access problems in areas with few practices)
Lower service quality in government-established clinics, which would be part of the estimated eﬀects
robustness_checks: Gradually richer speciﬁcations: quarter-relative-to-event and region dummies, then individual background characteristics, then individual ﬁxed eﬀects (columns 1‒3 of each outcome block)
Moving the pre-closure reference period back by three quarters and excluding the interval between it and the actual closure
Placebo analyses using outcomes measured prior to the actual closing (online supplement Tables B1‒B2)
Replication of the diﬀerence-in-diﬀerences strategy on the distance sample (online supplement Table B4)
Correcting for missing values by including dummies for missing values
Separating retirement-driven from non-retirement closures (Tables A3 and A4)
unresolved_confounders: The quality of service received in government-established clinics, which 'will comprise part of the eﬀects we estimate in our analyses below'
The relative weights of provider practice style versus disruption, which the authors state they cannot answer in a causal sense

estimator.value: OLS diﬀerence-in-diﬀerences with individual ﬁxed eﬀects (linear probability model for the 0/1 outcomes)

controls: Individual background characteristics (reported in the table as 'Individual background chars: Yes'; not itemized in the paper)

source_table.value: Table A4, Panel C, col (9), row 'Closure X Post'

adjustment_set.label: Individual background characteristics (not itemized in the paper)

heterogeneity.dimension: Reason for closure (physician retirement vs. other reasons)
heterogeneity.finding: This estimate is for closures classiﬁed as due to reasons other than retirement; the corresponding retirement estimate is in Table A3

nodes: eventual practice closure (within the observation window)

edges.from: eventual practice closure (within the observation window)

ambiguities: The point estimate is read from the 'Closure X Post' row of the richest speciﬁcation for this outcome (the column with individual ﬁxed eﬀects); the paper presents columns 1‒3 of each outcome block as a 'gradually richer speciﬁcation' and does not single one out as preferred.

The estimating equation printed in the paper is the event-study equation (1); no equation is printed for the minimalist diﬀerence-in-diﬀerence model whose 'Closure X Post' coeﬃcient the tables report, and the ﬁgure notes refer to that model as 'speciﬁcation (2)' while equation (2) in the text is the two-way ﬁxed-eﬀects practice-style model.

value.lhs: Y_it (the outcome of interest for individual i in quarter t relative to the (synthetic) closure)
value.parameter_of_interest: δ_j (the eﬀects of experiencing a clinic closure by quarter relative to j=-2); the tables report the collapsed 'Closure X Post' coeﬃcient of the minimalist diﬀerence-in-diﬀerence version of this model

index_sets.over: quarter relative to the (synthetic) practice closure

value.normalisation: δ_j and γ_j are measured relative to the reference quarter j = -2; quarter t = -1 is dropped from the formal analyses; in the ﬁgures eﬀects are measured relative to the quarterly mean in the penultimate year prior to closing (quarters -8 to -4 inclusive)

value.claimed_domain: A context where the patient is not left entirely without access to primary care ‒ i.e. a system such as the Danish one, in which patients are immediately re-matched and local governments are obligated by law to guarantee access to care
boundary_conditions: The patient is not left entirely without access to primary care
Access to care is secured by the local government (if no practice is open for intake, the local government must establish one)

theory_referenced: Continuity of care ‒ information, management and interpersonal continuity (Haggerty et al., 2003)
Physician practice style (Chandra et al., 2011)

falsification.condition: If varying the choice of reference period generates substantial diﬀerences in estimated eﬀects, this implies systematically diﬀerent pre-closure trends across treatment and comparison individuals that the regression model does not capture.

claims.statement: The practice (provider) ﬁxed eﬀect for 'Any Provider Visit' estimated on one random half of the sample predicts the ﬁxed eﬀect estimated on the other random half, with a slope below one that measures how much of the estimated variation in practice style is signal rather than sampling noise.

treatment.label: Practice (provider) ﬁxed eﬀect for 'Any Provider Visit' estimated on the second random subgroup

definition.value: Practice ﬁxed eﬀect γ̂_j^2 from the two-way ﬁxed-eﬀects model y_ijt = α_i + γ_j + τ_t + ε_ijt, estimated on the second of two random halves of the pre-closure sample; identiﬁed within the set of providers connected through patient mobility

timing.value: Estimated on data prior to practice closures, using observed practice switching well before closures

outcome.label: Practice (provider) ﬁxed eﬀect for 'Any Provider Visit' estimated on the ﬁrst random subgroup

definition.value: Practice ﬁxed eﬀect γ̂_j^1 from the same two-way ﬁxed-eﬀects model, estimated on the ﬁrst of the two random halves of the pre-closure sample

timing.value: Estimated on data prior to practice closures

units.value: Slope coeﬃcient, in units of the ﬁrst-subgroup ﬁxed eﬀect per unit of the second-subgroup ﬁxed eﬀect (both in the units of the underlying outcome); a reliability-type ratio

magnitude.interpretation: Correcting for measurement error turns out to be important in our setting – but the degree varies a lot across outcome domains.

estimand.target_population: Primary care practices (providers) in the connected set for which practice ﬁxed eﬀects can be identiﬁed from patient mobility before closures

population.description: Practices (providers) in the largest set connected through patient mobility before practice closures, constituting 99.3% of the sample; ﬁxed eﬀects estimated on pre-closure data for patients exposed to closures before they experience them, together with the comparison group
subgroups_defined: Two random halves of the sample used for the split-sample measurement-error correction
population.selection: Practices must be connected to the main set of practices through patient mobility before closures; newly established destination practices that only receive patients from one origin practice and never have patients leaving for a connected practice cannot be assigned a practice style

identification.source_of_variation: Observed patient mobility between practices well before practice closures, used to identify practice ﬁxed eﬀects; the split into two estimation groups is random

key_assumptions.assumption: No selection into a practice on unobserved time-varying patient characteristics: patient and practice ﬁxed eﬀects may be arbitrarily correlated (sorting on time-invariant unobservables is allowed), but the error term must be independent of the practice a patient is matched to.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Event studies in which the event-time indicators are interacted with the standardized provider ﬁxed eﬀect, used to verify ﬂat pre-trends (appendix Fig. A5); periods in the neighborhood of the break-up of the patient‒physician relationship are dummied out

key_assumptions.assumption: No patient-speciﬁc gains: the practice eﬀect is additive and common across patients (no patient-by-practice match eﬀects).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a limitation of the two-way ﬁxed-eﬀects setup; no test is reported

key_assumptions.assumption: Practice styles are identiﬁed only within sets of providers connected through patient mobility before closures; the largest connected set constitutes 99.3% of the sample.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Abowd et al. (1999); the paper reports the share of the sample in the largest connected set

key_assumptions.assumption: The sampling error in the two split-sample sets of estimated practice ﬁxed eﬀects is uncorrelated, so that their covariance equals the variance of the true practice style.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Ensured by the random assignment of the sample to the two groups (Drenik et al., 2020)

formal.as_written: cov (γ̂_j^1, γ̂_j^2) = cov(γ_j + ε_j^1, γ_j + ε_j^2) = cov(γ_j, γ_j) = V(γ_j) as long as cov(ε_j^1, ε_j^2) = 0

threats_discussed: Sampling variability in the estimated practice eﬀects (limited mobility bias; Andrews et al., 2008)
Selection into practices on time-varying unobserved patient characteristics
Patients diﬀering in health care utilization around switches for reasons such as residential relocation
robustness_checks: Split-sample measurement-error correction producing shrunken practice-style estimates
Event studies with event-time indicators interacted with the standardized provider ﬁxed eﬀect, to verify ﬂat pre-trends (Fig. A5)
unresolved_confounders: Patient-speciﬁc gains from a particular patient‒practice match, which the setup cannot allow for

estimator.value: OLS regression of the provider ﬁxed eﬀects estimated on the ﬁrst random subgroup on those estimated on the second random subgroup

ambiguities: Table A5 prints no signiﬁcance stars, p-values or number of observations, so statistically_significant is left null even though the printed coeﬃcient is many standard errors from zero.

The 'treatment' and 'outcome' of this regression are two estimated objects (provider ﬁxed eﬀects from two random halves of the sample); the relationship is a measurement-reliability statement rather than a causal eﬀect, and the paper does not describe it as causal.

The means and standard deviations in columns (1) and (2) of Table A5 refer to the full-sample original and shrunken ﬁxed-eﬀect distributions, not to the dependent variable of the column (3) regression, so they are not recorded as the baseline mean or outcome SD.

definition.value: Mean diﬀerence in the estimated (shrunken) provider practice style before and after the (synthetic) closure, for the treated and the comparison group: Δ^T_γ̂_j and Δ^C_γ̂_j. Practice styles are provider ﬁxed eﬀects γ_j from the two-way ﬁxed-eﬀects model (2) estimated on pre-closure data and corrected for measurement error by a split-sample procedure. The destination practice style is that of the ﬁrst assigned destination practice.

timing.value: Detrended quarterly outcome in the two years leading up to and following the (synthetic) closure

units.value: Share (of 1.00) of the total eﬀect variation |Δ^T_y − Δ^C_y| attributable to the change in provider practice style, from equation (3)

magnitude.interpretation: Ultimately, the decomposition shows that the main driver behind the estimated eﬀects of closure is the disruption itself.

population.description: Individuals exposed to a primary care practice closure in Denmark 1998‒2015 (811,649 individuals distributed across 770 closing practices) and a matched comparison group of 877,547 individuals who experience a practice closure three years into the future (915 practices); quarterly observations in a four-year window around the (synthetic) closure; practice styles are estimated on the connected set of providers (99.3% of the sample)
